opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think AI R&D is kind of the capability that unlocks all the other capabilities, so it's the one I'd most want early warning on.

Most dangerous capabilities you might worry about, like helping someone build a bioweapon or carrying out a sophisticated cyberattack, are concerning in themselves, but they're relatively bounded. You can at least imagine measuring them, seeing them coming, and putting mitigations in place. AI that can meaningfully do AI research is different, because it feeds back on itself. If you have AI systems that can do the work of top AI researchers, you can potentially run huge numbers of copies of them, working around the clock, improving the next generation of AI. That next generation does the research even better, and so on. You could go from "roughly human-level at AI research" to something much more capable in a very short period, maybe months or even less, rather than the years or decades we might otherwise expect.

That matters for a few reasons. First, it compresses the timeline for everything else. Whatever dangerous capabilities we're worried about down the line could arrive much faster than our institutions, safety research, and policy processes can adapt. The world gets very little time to notice what's happening and respond.

Second, it could happen fairly quietly. A lot of this would be going on inside one company's servers. It's not necessarily something the public or governments would see play out in real time, so if you're not specifically measuring for it, you might not know you've crossed that threshold until you're well past it.

Third, it raises the stakes on alignment and security enormously. If AI systems are doing much of the work of designing their successors, then any problems with their goals or reliability can propagate and compound, and humans are increasingly less able to check the work. And from a security standpoint, a model with strong AI R&D capabilities is an incredibly valuable thing to steal, because whoever has it could potentially leapfrog everyone else.

So when I think about "if-then" commitments, where if AI reaches a certain capability then certain protective measures must be in place, AI R&D is near the top of my list. It's the capability where, if you wait until it's clearly here to start preparing, you may simply be too late, because things could move faster than you can react. I'd much rather we have good evaluations for it and have the protections ready before we get there.

r001.rationale: It calls AI R&D the capability it would most want early warning on and says it can unlock other capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes AI doing AI research, producing better successors in a feedback loop that could rapidly accelerate progress.

r003.rationale: It says the acceleration could leave institutions and policymakers too little time to notice and respond to emerging threats.

r004.rationale: It does not state that AIs failing at AI R&D are probably not human-level at other R&D.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the reason I focus on AI research and development is that it's kind of the capability that unlocks all the others. If you think about what makes this technology potentially so transformative, and potentially so dangerous, a lot of it comes down to the possibility of a feedback loop. Right now, progress in AI is bottlenecked on humans — there's a limited number of people who can do frontier AI research, they can only work so many hours, they can only have so many ideas per year. If you get to a point where AI systems themselves can do a meaningful share of that work — designing experiments, writing the code, interpreting results, coming up with the next algorithmic improvement — then you've potentially removed that bottleneck. And you could get a situation where AI makes better AI, which makes better AI, and the pace of progress goes from something that's already pretty fast to something that's genuinely hard for institutions and people to keep up with.

So from my perspective, when you're trying to figure out "how close are we to the really scary or really transformative stuff?", the capability to automate AI R&D is one of the most informative things to track. It's more informative than, say, whether a model can pass some exam or write a nice essay, because those don't change the rate of change. AI R&D does.

There's also a second reason, which is more about the structure of the risk. A lot of the catastrophic scenarios people worry about — whether that's a misaligned system gaining a lot of power, or a small group of humans using AI to get a decisive advantage over everyone else — those scenarios tend to run through this same dynamic. The actor that gets to automated AI research first could pull dramatically ahead, and that compresses the time anyone has to notice problems and react. So it's both a leading indicator of how fast things might go, and it's sort of the mechanism by which things could go very badly.

And then the practical point is that it's actually somewhat measurable. You can ask: can this system do the kinds of tasks that a junior research engineer at a frontier lab does? Can it do them autonomously, over long time horizons, without a human checking every step? Companies can run evaluations on that, and I think it's one of the more concrete triggers you could build policy and safety commitments around — "if the model crosses this threshold on AI R&D tasks, then these additional safeguards kick in." That's a lot more tractable than trying to define "dangerous intelligence" in the abstract.

r001.rationale: It calls AI R&D automation an informative leading indicator of the pace of progress, but does not identify it as the most likely early warning of AI capability in general R&D.

r002.rationale: It describes a possible feedback loop that could accelerate progress, but does not state that AI R&D capability alone has a significant chance of triggering an explosion in progress.

r003.rationale: It says automated AI research could let an actor pull dramatically ahead and compress the time people and institutions have to notice problems and react.

r004.rationale: It does not state that AIs unable to perform AI R&D are probably not human-level at other forms of R&D.

astra-6.text:
I think AI research and development is a particularly important capability because it could create a feedback loop. If you have an AI system that can help you build better AI systems, then improvements in AI can lead to faster improvements in AI. That’s a different dynamic from having a system that’s very good at some particular economically useful task.

Imagine that you could run a large number of copies of a system that does the work of a very good AI researcher. Those copies could work on improving the algorithms, improving how efficiently you use the hardware, and figuring out how to train the next generation of models. If that next generation is better at research, the process could accelerate further.

That’s not a guarantee of an immediate explosion in capabilities. There could be bottlenecks involving hardware, experiments, or coordinating all that work. But it’s a reason to pay special attention to this capability: it could change how much time we have between seeing an impressive AI system and seeing something much more powerful. And that matters enormously for how much time we have to understand the risks and prepare.

r001.rationale: The response calls AI R&D important to watch, but does not identify it as the most likely early warning of AI capability in general R&D.

r002.rationale: It describes a possible feedback loop and faster progress, but does not say AI R&D capability alone has a significant chance of triggering an explosion in AI progress.

r003.rationale: It says faster progress could reduce time to understand risks and prepare, but does not state that people could be left without sufficient time to react to emerging threats.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that AIs unable to do AI R&D are probably not human-level at other R&D.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that AI research is a capability that could feed back on itself. If you have an AI system that’s very good at doing AI research, you can use it to build a better AI system, which can then help you build an even better one.

That doesn’t mean you necessarily get some instantaneous explosion. There could be bottlenecks involving compute, experiments, or manufacturing. But you could get a much faster pace of progress than we’re used to, because you’re automating the work that produces further progress.

And that makes it a particularly consequential capability to watch. A system might initially be limited in lots of other ways, but if it can substantially accelerate AI research and development, those limitations could change pretty quickly. So I’m interested not just in how impressive a system is today, but in how much it changes our ability to build the next generation.

r001.rationale: It calls AI R&D especially consequential to watch, but does not identify it as the most likely early warning of AI capability in general R&D.

r002.rationale: It describes AI R&D feedback and potentially much faster progress, but does not state that AI R&D capability alone has a significant chance of triggering an explosion in AI progress.

r003.rationale: It says progress could accelerate quickly, but does not mention people having insufficient time to react to emerging AI threats.

r004.rationale: It does not state that AIs unable to do AI R&D are probably not human-level at other R&D.
